lesson.title: Probing the Ceiling One Segment at a Time
lesson.summary: Congestion avoidance replaces slow start's exponential growth with a much gentler, linear increase, so TCP can keep probing for extra bandwidth without repeatedly overshooting the network's capacity.
lesson.body:
Once the congestion window reaches the slow start threshold, doubling the window every round trip becomes too risky. At that point, cwnd is presumed to be near the network's actual capacity, and exponential growth would blow past it quickly, likely causing a burst of packet loss across many segments at once. Congestion avoidance exists to slow the pace of growth right when it matters most, so that TCP approaches the ceiling gradually and can stop close to it rather than crashing through it.

The rule for congestion avoidance is additive increase: instead of adding one MSS to cwnd for every ACK, the sender adds roughly one MSS to cwnd only after a full window's worth of segments has been acknowledged, which works out to about one MSS of growth per round trip time. A common implementation increases cwnd by MSS multiplied by MSS divided by cwnd for each ACK received, which sums to approximately one MSS per RTT over a full window. Compare this to slow start's doubling: growth from N to 2N in one RTT during slow start versus growth from N to N+1 in one RTT during congestion avoidance. The difference in aggressiveness is enormous, and it is intentional.

Why linear and not some other shape? The logic is about risk near the edge of capacity. Early in a connection's life, under-guessing the network's capacity wastes round trips, so it is worth being aggressive since the cost of a mistake is small. Once cwnd is near ssthresh, however, the cost of overshooting is a burst of loss and a subsequent multiplicative cutback (a behavior detailed in the discussion of TCP Reno). Growing by just one segment per RTT means that if loss does occur, it happens only slightly beyond the network's true capacity rather than at double it, so the correction needed is smaller and the network recovers faster. This gentle probing is often described as testing the water: TCP nudges the window up a little, watches for a sign of trouble, and nudges again.

Extending the earlier trace: after slow start ends with cwnd = 8 at ssthresh = 8, congestion avoidance takes over. RTT 5: cwnd grows to about 9. RTT 6: about 10. RTT 7: about 11. This continues, adding one segment's worth of capacity per round trip, until eventually a loss event occurs, at which point the congestion window is cut back and ssthresh is updated to reflect the new, lower estimate of safe capacity, usually to about half the window size at the time of loss. The connection then resumes congestion avoidance from that reduced window, repeating the cycle of gentle increase followed by cutback. This repeating sawtooth pattern, rise slowly, drop sharply, rise slowly again, is the signature behavior of loss-based congestion control and is examined as a whole in the chapter on TCP Reno, once fast retransmit and fast recovery have been introduced.
